claims.text: In single-phase high-entropy alloys, hardness is predominantly governed by lattice distortions arising from atomic size mismatch.
In single-phase high-entropy alloys, strength is predominantly governed by lattice distortions arising from atomic size mismatch.
Lattice distortion caused by atomic size mismatch impedes dislocation motion.
Increasing average atomic size mismatch systematically increases hardness relative to an alloy with smaller size mismatch.
Increasing average atomic size mismatch systematically increases yield strength relative to an alloy with smaller size mismatch.
The proposed initial material is a single-phase, equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
The proposed initial alloy has a randomized atomic arrangement and moderate atomic size differences.
Elemental substitution can be used to vary average atomic size mismatch while processing, grain size, and phase stability are held constant.
X-ray diffraction line broadening can be used to quantify lattice strain associated with atomic size mismatch.
Local strain mapping can be used to characterize lattice distortion associated with atomic size mismatch.
Greater atomic size mismatch produces larger local lattice distortions.
Larger local lattice distortions act as barriers to dislocation glide.
Obstructing dislocation glide increases alloy hardness.
Obstructing dislocation glide increases alloy yield strength.
The proposed size-mismatch relationship is expected to hold at room temperature in single-phase HEAs without significant precipitation or microstructural heterogeneity.
At high temperatures or in multiphase regions, strengthening mechanisms other than lattice distortion may dominate.
Local chemical ordering may affect quantification of the atomic-size-mismatch contribution.
